SQLoom: Set-Contrastive Learning of Syntactic, Semantic, and Logical Dependencies for Text-to-SQL

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: the ACM Web Conference 2027; May 10–14, 2027; Dublin, IrelandISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2027/XXCCS: Information systems Question answeringCCS: Information systems Structured Query Language
Hao Fu email: haofu@vt.edu Affiliation: Virginia Tech , Degang Sun email: dgsun@cnic.cn Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences , Wan Wei email: wanwei@cnic.cn Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences , Jinxia Wei email: weijinxia@cnic.cn Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences , Chun Long email: longchun@cnic.cn Affiliation: Computer Network Information Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences and Peng Gao email: penggao@vt.edu Affiliation: Virginia Tech
2027
Abstract.

Text-to-SQL translates natural language questions into SQL queries, enabling database access without writing SQL. Fine-tuning open-weight large language models (LLMs) is cost-effective, but existing methods treat SQL as ordinary text and optimize token-level likelihood without explicitly modeling its syntactic, semantic, and logical requirements. Thus, a single incorrect alias or comparison operator can invalidate a query while contributing little to training loss. We propose SQLoom, a constraint-aware fine-tuning framework with supervision at three levels: syntactic validity under SQL grammar and database schema, semantic alignment between query decisions and the question, and logical consistency across dependent clause decisions. SQLoom extends supervised fine-tuning with a unified set-contrastive objective favoring sets of correct outputs over minimally different incorrect ones at each level. LLM agents propose this supervision, which a SQL parser and execution on counterexample databases verify. We also release Spider-Refined, a training dataset correcting 378 flawed Spider annotations and enriching database schemas. Experiments on Spider, BIRD, and three perturbed Spider variants show that SQLoom improves execution accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B from 62.9% zero-shot to 88.7% on Spider development, reaching 89.2% on Spider test and 73.4% on BIRD development. It outperforms fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and agent-based baselines with up to 70 billion parameters. On question perturbations, SQLoom loses at most 0.6 accuracy points versus up to 12.1 for agent-based methods. It generates SQL in a single pass at 0.42 s per query, 23×\times faster than a GPT-4-based agent method. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of set-contrastive supervision over token-level training.

Keywords: 
Text-to-SQL, Large Language Models, Constrained Fine-Tuning, Preference Optimization, Natural Language Interfaces to Databases

1. Introduction

Text-to-SQL translates natural language questions into executable SQL queries (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023b), enabling users without SQL expertise to query relational databases through natural language interfaces. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in text-to-SQL research, owing to their strong natural language understanding (Gao et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024). However, general-purpose LLMs are not specifically trained for this task, and they often generate queries that reference non-existent columns, misinterpret the question, or combine inconsistent clauses. To mitigate these errors, prompt-based agent methods equip LLMs with extensive error-correction mechanisms, such as self-correction (Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023; Askari et al., 2025), multi-agent refinement (Wang et al., 2025; Cen et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025), and candidate selection (Pourreza et al., 2025a). These mechanisms require multiple calls to proprietary LLMs per question, which increases latency and cost (Zhang et al., 2025) and hinders deployment in Web services with high query volumes. Efficient fine-tuning methods that equip general-purpose LLMs with SQL-specific competence are therefore needed.

Existing fine-tuning methods for text-to-SQL fall into three main categories (Hong et al., 2024). Data-centric methods enlarge the training corpus through SQL-centric pre-training (Li et al., 2024b) and data synthesis (Yang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Each sample still teaches a single reference string, so the model has to infer the rules of SQL from millions of samples, e.g., 2.5M for OmniSQL (Li et al., 2025). Task-decomposition methods add auxiliary tasks or stages such as schema linking and skeleton parsing (Li et al., 2023c; Pourreza and Rafiei, 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025). They help the model select tables and columns, but the query itself is still learned by imitating one reference token by token. Feedback-driven methods optimize execution-based preferences or rewards with DPO or reinforcement learning (Zhai et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Pourreza et al., 2025b; Yao et al., 2026). A reward judges the whole query, so it cannot tell which part caused an error, and it still rewards a wrong query when its error does not affect the result on the given database. Most of these methods treat SQL as ordinary text, and even structure-aware rewards (Ma et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026) score a complete query instead of contrasting the tokens, decisions, and dependent clauses where errors occur.

Without supervision from this structure, the current fine-tuning paradigm faces three challenges, illustrated in Figure 1. C1 Syntactic validity. A query must use only defined tables, columns, and aliases. The first query in Figure 1 selects T3.name, but no table is named T3. PICARD (Scholak et al., 2021) filters such tokens with a parser during decoding, but the model still prefers them and needs the parser at deployment. C2 Semantic alignment. Each phrase of the question must map to the correct SQL fragment. “Different courses” requires COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) and “at least two” requires >= 2, whereas the second query writes COUNT(*) > 2. Schema-linking objectives (Qin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025) teach the model which tables and columns to use, but not which aggregates and operators. C3 Logical consistency. Dependent clauses must change together. The third query joins section, which yields one row per course section, but keeps COUNT(*), so a course is counted several times. Each clause looks reasonable alone, and the query often returns the correct result on the test database, so execution rewards miss it.

To tackle these challenges, we propose SQLoom, a constraint-aware fine-tuning framework. Our key insight is that SQL generation is better supervised by contrasting sets of outputs than by imitating a single reference. Owing to the grammar and the schema, a question often has several correct queries, and at many positions the correct output is a class of tokens, e.g., the columns of the joined tables after SELECT, rather than one token. Token-level SFT rewards one member and pushes down the others, including correct ones. SQLoom therefore augments SFT with a set-contrastive objective that favors a set of correct outputs over a set of wrong outputs differing from them at a single place, at three granularities. Syntactic constraint for C1. At each position, the correct set contains the tokens allowed by the grammar and the schema, and the wrong set contains the rest. Semantic constraint for C2. For each question phrase, the correct set contains its reference SQL fragment, e.g., >= 2 for “at least two”, and the wrong set contains fragments the model confuses with it, e.g., > 2. Logical constraint for C3. For each pair of dependent clauses, we edit the question so that one clause must change, e.g., counting only courses with a lab section. The correct set contains the query that also updates the dependent clause, e.g., the count, and the wrong set contains the query that changes only the edited clause. The three constraints thus address the three challenges by teaching which tokens are legal, which fragments match the question, and which clauses must change together.

Our technical contributions are summarized below.

  • •

    We propose SQLoom, which replaces token-by-token imitation of one reference query with set-contrastive supervision labeled by a parser and query execution, instantiated as three constraints on syntax, semantics, and logic.

  • •

    We design a syntactic constraint that uses the parse state as a training signal. An incremental parser with schema scope derives the legal tokens at each position, and a trie over schema identifiers aligns grammar terminals with subword tokens, so the model learns the grammar in training and needs no parser to correct its output at inference.

  • •

    We design a semantic constraint that teaches the model to map each question phrase to the correct SQL fragment rather than a confusable one. It grounds question phrases in the AST nodes that realize them and contrasts each node with confusions mined from the model’s own errors.

  • •

    We design a logical constraint that keeps dependent clauses consistent when one of them changes. It derives these dependencies from a dependency graph over clauses and contrasts consistent and inconsistent queries on counterexample databases where their results differ.

Constructing these constraints requires correct and wrong sets for every training example, which are absent from the original annotations. The syntactic sets are derived directly by the parser, whereas the semantic and logical sets are built by a constraint synthesizer with four LLM agents. For the semantic constraint, an error-mining agent finds the model’s wrong decisions and an alignment agent maps question phrases to SQL fragments with their confusions. For the logical constraint, an editing agent rewrites the question along a dependency edge with the two queries, and a verification agent checks the edited query’s intent. Each output must pass the parser and execution checks. While synthesizing constraints in our experiments, the error-mining agent also flagged 378 Spider annotations that mislabel correct predictions or teach incorrect queries. After manual review, we correct these annotations and release Spider-Refined, a training dataset that extends Spider with the corrected annotations, schema descriptions generated by the synthesizer, and the verified constraint samples. Spider-Refined serves only as training data, and all evaluations use the official labels. Experiments lead to four findings.

  • •

    The gains come from the objective. With the same training data, replacing the constraints with plain SFT lowers EX by 8.8 points on Spider Test and 10.3 points on BIRD Dev.

  • •

    A 1.7B model outperforms much larger systems. SQLoom reaches 88.7% EX on Spider Dev (62.9% zero-shot), 89.2% on Spider Test, and 73.4% on BIRD Dev, above all evaluated baselines and zero-shot Qwen3-235B and GPT-4.

  • •

    SQLoom is robust to perturbed questions. It loses at most 0.6 points on the three Spider variants, whereas agent-based methods lose 8.8–12.1 points on Spider-DK.

  • •

    SQLoom is efficient. It generates SQL in one pass (0.42 s per query), 23×\times faster than CogSQL with GPT-4 in our setup.

Overall, these results show that with constraint-based supervision, even a small LLM can generate SQL accurately and robustly.

2. Background

2.1. Problem Formulation

Given a natural language question qq and a database 𝒟\mathcal{D} with schema 𝒮\mathcal{S} (tables, columns, primary and foreign keys), text-to-SQL generates a query y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T}) whose execution result on 𝒟\mathcal{D} answers qq. Let x=(q,𝒮)x=(q,\mathcal{S}) denote the model input. Fine-tuning methods train an LLM pθp_{\theta} by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of a reference query y∗y^{*},

(1) ℒSFT=−∑t=1Tlogpθ(yt∗∣x,y<t∗).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_{\theta}\left(y^{*}_{t}\mid x,y^{*}_{<t}\right).

2.2. Related Work

Prompt-based Agent Methods. Early neural parsers encode the schema with task-specific architectures (Zhong et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023a). LLM-based methods instead improve a general model at inference, through example selection, decomposition, and schema pruning (Gao et al., 2024; Pourreza and Rafiei, 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Qu et al., 2024; Talaei et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a), or through agents that plan, refine, and select among candidates (Wang et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Askari et al., 2025; Cen et al., 2025; Pourreza et al., 2025a; Shkapenyuk et al., 2025). Other work checks SQL with tools rather than with a model. Constrained decoding runs an incremental SQL parser during generation and discards tokens that violate the grammar or the schema (Scholak et al., 2021), and test-suite evaluation executes a predicted query on several generated databases to expose queries that are correct only by coincidence on the original one (Zhong et al., 2020). In essence, these methods repair or detect errors after generation instead of preventing them. The repair is judged by the same LLM or by execution failures, so a query that executes but answers another question often passes, and each question pays for several LLM calls (Zhang et al., 2025). The tools also act outside training, so the model does not learn from them and the parser must stay in the serving loop.

Data-centric Fine-tuning. This direction scales the training corpus through SQL-centric pre-training and data synthesis (Sun et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Its limitation lies in the form of supervision rather than its amount (Table 1). Each sample still provides one reference string, so the model must infer grammar rules, question-to-SQL bindings, and clause dependencies statistically, and equivalent queries for one question even provide conflicting targets.

Task-decomposition Fine-tuning. This direction splits generation into schema linking, skeleton parsing, and SQL stages, or adds them as auxiliary tasks (Li et al., 2023c; Pourreza and Rafiei, 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025). It strengthens the recognition of the input, namely which tables and columns to use (Table 1), but leaves output-side decisions, such as aggregates, operators, and their consistency across clauses, to token-level imitation.

Feedback-driven Fine-tuning. This direction optimizes execution-based preferences or rewards with DPO or reinforcement learning (Rafailov et al., 2023; Zhai et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Pourreza et al., 2025b; Yao et al., 2026), and recent work refines the reward with graph, AST, or clause-level matching (Weng et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026). The core problem is the signal itself. An outcome-level reward spreads the same credit over all tokens, and single-database execution wrongly rewards inconsistent queries with correct results (Table 1).

2.3. Motivation

Problem measurement. To measure which errors remain under standard fine-tuning, we fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B on the Spider training set with LoRA and token-level SFT, and classify its 211 model errors on the Spider development set (Figure 2; categories in Appendix D). Wrong columns dominate from medium to extra-hard questions, followed by semantic errors. These queries are valid but bind a question element to a wrong decision, which typically spans only one or a few tokens.

These model errors trace back to Eq. 1, which raises the likelihood of the reference without explicitly penalizing incorrect outputs and ignores three properties of SQL. 1) Validity is decidable. Given the grammar and the schema, an incremental parser determines which tokens are legal at each position, yet SFT does not explicitly lower the probability of illegal ones. 2) Errors are local but decisive. A wrong decision, such as COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT ⋅\cdot), occupies a small share of the SFT loss but changes the answer; conversely, since SQL labels are not unique, an equivalent rewriting of y∗y^{*} is penalized as much as a wrong query. 3) Decisions are dependent. A one-to-many join may require DISTINCT, and GROUP BY must follow the target entity, but a query that violates such a dependency can still return the correct result on the given database.

Requirements. A fine-tuning objective for SQL should therefore meet three requirements. First, it contrasts the reference with outputs certified to be wrong by a parser or by execution beyond the given database. Second, it confines the contrast to the structural unit in which the outputs differ. Third, it applies at the level of tokens, decisions, and dependent decisions.

3. Methodology

3.1. Overview

Token-level SFT maximizes the likelihood of the reference without penalizing incorrect outputs, so wrong tokens, wrong decisions, and inconsistent clauses receive little training signal. SQLoom supervises these errors explicitly while keeping single-pass inference. As shown in Figure 3, the constraint synthesizer (Section 4.1) builds sets of correct outputs and minimally different wrong outputs at the syntactic, semantic, and logical levels. A set-contrastive objective favors the correct set over the wrong set at each of the three levels. A three-stage procedure trains the model with this objective.

Three-level correctness hierarchy. The three challenges occur at different granularities, so one loss on the whole query cannot tell where an error lies. We therefore define one unit per challenge, namely a token for C1, a decision for C2, and a pair of dependent decisions for C3. A decision is the SQL fragment that realizes one element of the question, e.g., >= 2 for “at least two”, and corresponds to a node of the abstract syntax tree (AST) of the query. A logical unit links two decisions in different clauses, e.g., a join and the count that depends on it.

Oracle-certified constraints. Since one question can have several correct queries, comparing an output with the reference cannot tell whether the output is wrong or merely written differently. For each unit uu we therefore build a constraint c=(𝒫c,𝒩c,Mc)c=(\mathcal{P}_{c},\mathcal{N}_{c},M_{c}), where 𝒫c\mathcal{P}_{c} is a set of correct (admissible) outputs, 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c} is a set of wrong (inadmissible) outputs that differ from them only in uu, and Mc​(y)M_{c}(y) marks the token positions of yy that belong to uu. Wrong outputs are certified by an oracle, i.e., a program with a definite answer rather than a learned model, whereas correct outputs are references or pass additional checks. The oracle is a schema-aware SQL parser at the syntactic level. At the other two levels it executes the queries on the original database 𝒟\mathcal{D} and on counterexample databases {𝒟j′}\{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}_{j}\}, i.e., small generated databases on which similar queries return different results. Appendix C details both oracles.

Set-contrastive objective. We compare outputs only at the positions of their unit. Let rθ​(y,M)=∑t∈Mlog⁡pθ​(yt∣x,y<t)pref​(yt∣x,y<t)r_{\theta}(y,M)=\sum_{t\in M}\log\frac{p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})} be how much more likely the model makes yy at positions MM than a frozen reference model prefp_{\mathrm{ref}}, here the model after warm-up. Each constraint is enforced by

(2) ℓ⁡(c)=−log⁡∑y∈𝒫cexp⁡(β​rθ​(y,Mc​(y)))∑y∈𝒫c∪𝒩cexp⁡(β​rθ​(y,Mc​(y))),\ell(c)=-\log\frac{\sum_{y\in\mathcal{P}_{c}}\exp\big(\beta\,r_{\theta}(y,M_{c}(y))\big)}{\sum_{y\in\mathcal{P}_{c}\cup\mathcal{N}_{c}}\exp\big(\beta\,r_{\theta}(y,M_{c}(y))\big)},

which raises the total probability of the correct set over the wrong set at the positions of the unit, while the rest of the query keeps the plain SFT signal. The temperature β\beta controls how sharply the two sets are separated. The full objective is

(3) ℒ=ℒSFT+∑k∈{syn,sem,log}λk​ℒk,ℒk=∑c∈𝒞kℓ⁡(c),\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}+\sum_{k\in\{\mathrm{syn},\mathrm{sem},\mathrm{log}\}}\lambda_{k}\,\mathcal{L}_{k},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{k}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\ell(c),

where 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} is the set of constraints at level kk, and ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}} covers the references and all admissible outputs. Table 2 lists the instantiations.

Semantic negatives are valid queries, and logical negatives also keep each decision consistent with the question (last row of Table 2), so each level covers errors that the previous levels miss. The loss never penalizes equivalent outputs and updates only the constrained unit (Appendix A).

3.2. Syntactic Constraint

The syntactic constraint teaches the model which tokens may come next (C1). Legality depends on the grammar and the schema, e.g., an alias defined inside a subquery is not visible outside it, and SQL keywords and names do not align with the LLM’s subword tokens.

We feed y∗y^{*} token by token into an incremental parser, i.e., a SQL parser that can analyze an unfinished query, extended with the schema. After each prefix y<t∗y^{*}_{<t}, the parser returns a state sts_{t} that records what may come next and which tables, aliases, and columns are visible. The legal set 𝒱valid​(st)\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{valid}}(s_{t}) contains each token vv after which the query can still be completed into a valid one, e.g., only table names of 𝒮\mathcal{S} after FROM. Since a name may span several subword tokens, legality is checked on the decoded text with a prefix tree (trie) of keywords and schema names, so the partial name stu of student counts as legal. The constraint is applied at decision positions 𝒯d\mathcal{T}_{d}, i.e., the first token of each keyword, name, operator, or parenthesis, and the legal sets are cached per database.

The syntactic instance of Eq. 2 is

(4) ℒsyn=−∑t∈𝒯dlog∑v∈𝒱valid​(st)pθ(v∣x,y<t∗),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{syn}}=-\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{d}}\log\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{valid}}(s_{t})}p_{\theta}\left(v\mid x,y^{*}_{<t}\right),

which moves probability from illegal tokens to the whole legal set rather than to the reference token alone, so legal alternatives are not pushed down. The model thus learns validity during training and needs no parser at inference.

3.3. Semantic Constraint

The semantic constraint binds each element of the question to the SQL decision that realizes it (C2). Datasets do not annotate which phrase maps to which part of the query, and a seemingly wrong alternative may be an equivalent rewrite.

For each training example, we extract alignments 𝒜={(ei,di)}\mathcal{A}=\{(e_{i},d_{i})\}, where eie_{i} is an element of qq, e.g., “at least two”, and did_{i} is the AST node of y∗y^{*} that realizes it, e.g., >= 2 (Figure 9). Elements fall into six types, namely entity, attribute, value, aggregation, comparison/quantifier, and ordering. An alignment is kept only if replacing did_{i} by another option of the same type changes the execution result, which confirms that did_{i} depends on eie_{i}. As an auxiliary task, the model writes the alignment list before the SQL, supervised by ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}.

For each alignment, 𝒫c={y∗}\mathcal{P}_{c}=\{y^{*}\}, and 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c} contains confusions y~\tilde{y} that replace did_{i} with a similar but wrong option, e.g., a similar column, COUNT(*) for COUNT(DISTINCT ⋅\cdot), or > for >=. Candidates are ranked by how often the current model makes them, so training targets its actual mistakes. Only valid confusions that return a different result from y∗y^{*} are kept, so equivalent rewrites are not penalized by design. With one confusion per unit, Eq. 2 reduces to the pairwise loss of direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) restricted to the tokens of did_{i}, which corrects the wrong decision without changing the rest of the query.

3.4. Logical Constraint

The logical constraint teaches the model to update dependent clauses together (C3). A single training pair rarely shows how one clause should change when another changes, and an inconsistent query often returns the correct result on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, so executing it there does not reveal the error.

We split a query into components (FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, aggregation, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY/LIMIT, and sub-queries) and build a graph GG in which an edge states that a certain change to one component requires checking another (Figure 4; all edges in Table 4). For example, adding a one-to-many join requires checking whether the count still counts each entity once. Each edge is a unit. Edges mark what may change, and execution decides how.

Starting from (q,y∗)(q,y^{*}), we change one aligned element of the question and generate an edited question q′q^{\prime}, a propagated query y′y^{\prime} in which the edited component and the components that depend on it are updated, and a partially propagated query y~′\tilde{y}^{\prime} in which only the edited component changes. Then 𝒫c={y′}\mathcal{P}_{c}=\{y^{\prime}\} and 𝒩c={y~′}\mathcal{N}_{c}=\{\tilde{y}^{\prime}\} for input (q′,𝒮)(q^{\prime},\mathcal{S}). For example, restricting the running example to courses with a lab section adds a join with section; y′y^{\prime} counts DISTINCT T2.course_id, whereas y~′\tilde{y}^{\prime} keeps COUNT(*), which counts a course per lab section. The pair isolates the dependency and is kept only if the two queries differ on a counterexample database, y′y^{\prime} runs on all databases, and the verification agent judges y′y^{\prime} consistent with q′q^{\prime}.

The mask McM_{c} covers the components that differ between y′y^{\prime} and y~′\tilde{y}^{\prime}. Since both queries contain the edit, the loss focuses on the components that must change because of it. Eq. 2 again reduces to a DPO-style loss on these positions, and y′y^{\prime} is also added to ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}. Appendices B, C, and E show examples of all levels.

3.5. Training Procedure

The training procedure combines the three constraints in one model. Preference losses are unstable before the model can write reasonable SQL, and later fine-tuning stages tend to overwrite earlier skills. SQLoom therefore trains in three stages (Algorithm 1). Stage 1 is a short SFT warm-up whose result also serves as prefp_{\mathrm{ref}}. Stage 2 trains with Eq. 3. Stage 3 prepends to each input the kk most similar verified question–query pairs of the same database, since Web applications answer many questions over one database. After each stage, the model is further fine-tuned on queries corrected by the error-mining agent AeA_{e} (Section 4.1), mixed with a share of earlier examples (replay), and its weights are averaged with the pre-trained ones as in WiSE-FT (Wortsman et al., 2022) to reduce forgetting.

4. Verified Constraint Synthesis

4.1. Agent-based Constraint Synthesizer

The constraint synthesizer instantiates the constraints of Section 3.1. As shown in Figure 5, four LLM agents propose candidates, and the grammar and execution oracles decide their membership in 𝒫c\mathcal{P}_{c} or 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c}. The parser alone yields the syntactic constraint, AeA_{e} and AaA_{a} the semantic one, and AdA_{d} and AvA_{v} the logical one.

  • •

    Error-mining agent AeA_{e}. After each stage, AeA_{e} finds the wrong decision in each failed training prediction and writes a close correction, repaired by execution for at most imaxci^{c}_{\max} rounds. Corrections serve as SFT examples, the wrong decisions select the units for semantic and logical constraints, and suspicious references are flagged for manual review.

  • •

    Alignment agent AaA_{a} proposes semantic units (alignments) and up to three confusable alternatives per decision.

  • •

    Editing agent AdA_{d} samples a logical unit (an edge of GG) and produces q′q^{\prime}, y′y^{\prime}, and y~′\tilde{y}^{\prime}.

  • •

    Verification agent AvA_{v} back-translates y′y^{\prime} into a question and checks whether it matches q′q^{\prime}.

Counterexample database generation. Given a database 𝒟\mathcal{D} and two queries y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} with the same result on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the generator searches for a database 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} that satisfies the constraints of 𝒟\mathcal{D} and on which y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} return different results. It (1) samples a sub-database containing the tables referenced by the queries, following foreign keys to keep referential integrity; (2) mutates it by duplicating rows with fresh primary keys, perturbing values at the boundaries of query constants (e.g., 22 in >= 2), and inserting additional child rows into one-to-many relationships; and (3) keeps a mutated instance if it satisfies the primary-key, foreign-key, NOT NULL, and type constraints and separates the two queries. Duplicated child rows expose join-induced double counting, boundary values expose inclusive versus exclusive comparisons, and ties expose superlative and LIMIT errors. The search stops when a separating instance is found or a mutation budget is exhausted. The same procedure is used for the non-equivalence check of confusions and the substitution test of alignments. Each training example contributes at most one pair per edge type in Table 4.

Because each candidate must pass checks that do not depend on an LLM, agent errors reduce the amount of data rather than its correctness. For example, an incorrect alignment fails the substitution test, an incorrect propagated query is not separated from its partial counterpart, and an equivalent confusion is discarded. The agent prompts are listed in Appendix F.

4.2. The Spider-Refined Dataset

During error mining, many apparent model errors turned out to be Spider annotation problems. We manually reviewed all cases flagged by AeA_{e} and introduce Spider-Refined, a training dataset built from Spider that corrects these annotations, enriches the database schemas, and adds the verified alignments, confusions, and counterfactual pairs produced by the constraint synthesizer. Spider-Refined is used only for training; evaluation uses the official sets.

Among the confirmed annotation issues, the most frequent is a correct prediction that is rejected by execution-based comparison (163 cases), followed by under-specified questions whose references return extra (71) or missing (37) columns, and references whose logic contradicts the question (31). Figure 14 lists all issue types. For each confirmed issue, the reference query or the question is minimally revised; when several outputs are equally valid, the alternatives are recorded. All revisions are verified by execution.

Spider schemas often use terse or ambiguous identifiers. For each database, the synthesizer agents generate descriptions of (i) table semantics, e.g., player stores player records; (ii) value types, e.g., REAL for continuous values such as income and INTEGER for counts; (iii) relationships, e.g., one club has many players; (iv) potential pitfalls, e.g., a floating-point primary key that makes equality comparison unreliable; and (v) intended use cases, e.g., retrieving the players of a club or aggregating income per club. The descriptions are checked manually and added to the schema input 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the agent prompts.

5. Experiments

We evaluate how SQLoom compares with fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and agent-based methods and with general-purpose LLMs, its robustness to perturbed questions and unseen datasets, how each component contributes, and its cost.

5.1. Experimental Settings

Datasets. We use Spider (Yu et al., 2018) (10,181 questions, 200 databases, 138 domains), its variants Spider-DK (Gan et al., 2021a), Spider-Syn (Gan et al., 2021b), and Spider-Realistic (Deng et al., 2020), and BIRD (Li et al., 2023b) (12,751 pairs, 95 databases, 33.4 GB). We train two models, one on the Spider-Refined training set, evaluated on Spider and its variants, and one on the BIRD training set, evaluated on BIRD. Evaluation databases are disjoint from training databases, so all evaluations are cross-database. Spider difficulty levels follow the official script, which counts SQL components such as joins, aggregations, and nested queries.

Baselines. We compare with fine-tuning methods (T5-3B+PICARD (Scholak et al., 2021), RESDSQL (Li et al., 2023c), SQL-PaLM (Sun et al., 2023), CodeS (Li et al., 2024b), SENSE (Yang et al., 2024), ROUTE (Qin et al., 2025), OmniSQL (Li et al., 2025), and JOLT-SQL (Song et al., 2025)), preference and RL methods (ExCoT (Zhai et al., 2025), SQL-R1 (Ma et al., 2025), and Arctic-Text2SQL-R1 (Yao et al., 2026)), and agent-based methods (SQLFixAgent (Cen et al., 2025), DEA-SQL (Xie et al., 2024), SuperSQL (Li et al., 2024a), CogSQL (Yuan et al., 2025), TA-SQL (Qu et al., 2024), and AskData (Shkapenyuk et al., 2025)).

Metrics and implementation. We report execution accuracy (EX). SQLoom fine-tunes Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on one RTX 4090 GPU and decodes greedily without constrained decoding. The agents use GPT-4. We set λsyn=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{syn}}=0.5, λsem=λlog=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{sem}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{log}}=1.0, β=0.1\beta=0.1, and k=3k=3, selected by grid search on a held-out 10% of the training set (Appendix C). Results of SQLoom are averaged over 3 seeds.

5.2. Main Results

As shown in Table 3, SQLoom achieves the best EX on all three sets with the smallest model, exceeding the strongest baselines by 1.1, 0.4, and 4.5 points. It outperforms JOLT-SQL, the best fine-tuning method, by 13.0 points on BIRD, and AskData, the best agent-based method, by 6.0 points, without proprietary LLM calls.

As Table 3 and Figure 13 show, all baselines above 85% on the Spider test set or 60% on BIRD use at least 7B parameters, whereas SQLoom uses 1.7B. Its margin is largest on BIRD, whose questions involve more clauses and more chances for inconsistency.

Unlike most baselines, SQLoom does not use the external knowledge evidence of BIRD; adding it raises EX to 76.8%. The gains are also not explained by imitating the teacher, since oracles vet agent outputs and GPT-4 is weaker on the Spider variants (Figure 6a).

5.3. Comparison with General-Purpose LLMs

Figure 8 shows that model size does not determine zero-shot accuracy. Qwen3-8B matches Qwen3-235B, and the open-weight DeepSeek-V3 is 14.4 points lower. Reasoning and code-specialized models score lowest; most of their failures lack a final SQL statement within the generation budget, which is why the longer-reasoning DeepSeek-R1-671B scores below DeepSeek-R1-8B. SQLoom lifts Qwen3-1.7B from 62.9% to 88.7%, i.e., 13.4 points above the best zero-shot model, which is 138×\times larger.

5.4. Robustness and Transfer

On Spider-DK, Spider-Syn, and Spider-Realistic (Figure 6a,b), SQLoom loses at most 0.6 points relative to Spider Dev, whereas agent-based methods lose 8.8–12.1 points on Spider-DK and 8.9 points on Spider-Syn. Lexical matching between question and schema breaks under domain knowledge and synonyms, whereas SQLoom grounds question elements in verified decisions.

In the cross-dataset setting (Figure 6c), SQLoom improves over SFT trained on the same data by 8.8 points from Spider to BIRD and 5.8 points from BIRD to Spider. Training on Spider-Refined instead of Spider improves EX on the official sets by 1.2 and 1.4 points (Figure 6d), so the corrections help beyond evaluation.

5.5. Ablation Study

All training stages contribute. Removing constraint training costs 12.5 and 9.7 points, and removing error-mined correction costs 11.1 and 17.2 points (Figure 7a). Removing the SFT warm-up hurts most.

Each constraint level helps; the semantic and logical constraints contribute most, especially on BIRD. Replacing all constraints with SFT on the same data loses 8.8 and 10.3 points. Single-stage mixing loses 3.6 and 5.3 points, as its reference model lacks the warm-up.

5.6. Analysis and Cost

In Figure 7b, the SFT warm-up mainly helps hard and extra-hard questions (+15.0 and +21.7 points), where the base model often fails to produce well-formed SQL. Constraint training brings the largest gains at each level, especially for medium to extra-hard questions (+31.6 to +43.0 points). As a result, the gap between easy and extra-hard questions shrinks from 53.7 to 9.6 points. Context augmentation adds a further 0.7–2.1 points. Finally, EX varies by at most 1.4 points over the tested values of β\beta and λlog\lambda_{\mathrm{log}} (Figure 10).

SQLoom moves the agent cost to training (Figure 7c,d). Training takes 10.8 GPU hours (2.3×\times SFT) and 21.3 GB of memory, plus 38K GPT-4 calls. Inference is as fast as SFT (0.42 s per query) and 23×\times faster than CogSQL with GPT-4.

6. Conclusion and Future Work

We propose SQLoom, which enforces the syntactic validity, semantic alignment, and logical consistency of SQL with oracle-verified set-contrastive supervision, and release the Spider-Refined dataset. With 1.7B parameters, SQLoom outperforms larger fine-tuned, RL, and agent-based systems in a single pass.

In future work, we will fine-tune larger open-weight LLMs with SQLoom to study how constraint-based supervision scales with model size, and construct more constraints, e.g., for nested queries and other SQL dialects.

Appendix A Properties of the Set-Contrastive Objective

This appendix explains why Eq. 2 is a suitable training objective for all three levels. We show two properties. First, Eq. 2 unifies existing losses: the syntactic loss of Eq. 4 and the DPO loss are its special cases (Proposition A.1), so one objective serves all levels. Second, its gradient pushes down only oracle-certified negatives and fades once a constraint is satisfied (Proposition A.2), so equivalent queries are never penalized and training focuses on unsatisfied constraints.

Notation. We analyze a single constraint c=(𝒫c,𝒩c,Mc)c=(\mathcal{P}_{c},\mathcal{N}_{c},M_{c}), write ry=rθ​(y,Mc​(y))r_{y}=r_{\theta}(y,M_{c}(y)), and define

π⁡(y)=eβ​ry∑y′∈𝒫c∪𝒩ceβ​ry′,π⁡(𝒩c)=∑y∈𝒩cπ⁡(y),\displaystyle\pi(y)=\frac{e^{\beta r_{y}}}{\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{c}\cup\mathcal{N}_{c}}e^{\beta r_{y^{\prime}}}},\qquad\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c})=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{N}_{c}}\pi(y),
π𝒫​(y)=eβ​ry∑y′∈𝒫ceβ​ry′(y∈𝒫c).\displaystyle\pi_{\mathcal{P}}(y)=\frac{e^{\beta r_{y}}}{\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{c}}e^{\beta r_{y^{\prime}}}}\quad(y\in\mathcal{P}_{c}).

Intuitively, π⁡(y)\pi(y) is the share of candidate yy among all candidates, π𝒫​(y)\pi_{\mathcal{P}}(y) is its share among the positives, and π⁡(𝒩c)\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}) is the total share of the negatives, so ℓ⁡(c)\ell(c) is small when π⁡(𝒩c)\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}) is small.

The first proposition recovers existing losses from Eq. 2.

Proposition A.1 (Special cases).

(a) At the syntactic level, with candidates y<t∗⊕vy^{*}_{<t}\oplus v for v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, β=1\beta=1, and pref≡1p_{\mathrm{ref}}\equiv 1, Eq. 2 equals the syntactic loss of Eq. 4 at position tt. (b) If 𝒫c={y+}\mathcal{P}_{c}=\{y^{+}\} and 𝒩c={y−}\mathcal{N}_{c}=\{y^{-}\}, Eq. 2 equals −log⁡σ⁡(β⁡(ry+−ry−))-\log\sigma\big(\beta(r_{y^{+}}-r_{y^{-}})\big), a DPO loss (Rafailov et al., 2023) whose reward is restricted to the positions McM_{c}.

Proof.

(a) With β=1\beta=1 and pref≡1p_{\mathrm{ref}}\equiv 1, exp⁡(ry)=pθ​(v∣x,y<t∗)\exp(r_{y})=p_{\theta}(v\mid x,y^{*}_{<t}). Since 𝒫c∪𝒩c\mathcal{P}_{c}\cup\mathcal{N}_{c} covers 𝒱\mathcal{V}, the denominator equals ∑v∈𝒱pθ​(v∣x,y<t∗)=1\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p_{\theta}(v\mid x,y^{*}_{<t})=1, and the numerator is the probability mass of 𝒱valid​(st)\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{valid}}(s_{t}). (b) Dividing the numerator and the denominator by exp⁡(β​ry+)\exp(\beta r_{y^{+}}) gives ℓ⁡(c)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−β⁡(ry+−ry−)))=−log⁡σ⁡(β⁡(ry+−ry−))\ell(c)=\log\big(1+\exp(-\beta(r_{y^{+}}-r_{y^{-}}))\big)=-\log\sigma\big(\beta(r_{y^{+}}-r_{y^{-}})\big). ∎

The second proposition characterizes how Eq. 2 updates the masked reward ryr_{y} of each candidate.

Proposition A.2 (Gradient).

ℓ⁡(c)=−log⁡(1−π⁡(𝒩c))≥0\ell(c)=-\log\big(1-\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c})\big)\geq 0, and

(5) ∂ℓ⁡(c)∂ry={β​π​(y)≥0,y∈𝒩c,β⁡(π⁡(y)−π𝒫​(y))≤0,y∈𝒫c.\frac{\partial\ell(c)}{\partial r_{y}}=\begin{cases}\beta\,\pi(y)\geq 0,&y\in\mathcal{N}_{c},\\ \beta\big(\pi(y)-\pi_{\mathcal{P}}(y)\big)\leq 0,&y\in\mathcal{P}_{c}.\end{cases}

The total gradient magnitudes over 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c} and 𝒫c\mathcal{P}_{c} both equal β​π​(𝒩c)\beta\,\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}).

Proof.

Write

ℓ(c)=−log∑y∈𝒫ceβ​ry+log∑y∈𝒫c∪𝒩ceβ​ry.\ell(c)=-\log\sum_{y\in\mathcal{P}_{c}}e^{\beta r_{y}}+\log\sum_{y\in\mathcal{P}_{c}\cup\mathcal{N}_{c}}e^{\beta r_{y}}.

The first claim follows from the definition of π\pi. Differentiating the second term gives β​π​(y)\beta\pi(y) for each candidate, and differentiating the first gives −β​π𝒫​(y)-\beta\pi_{\mathcal{P}}(y) for y∈𝒫cy\in\mathcal{P}_{c}. Since π⁡(y)=π𝒫​(y)​(1−π⁡(𝒩c))≤π𝒫​(y)\pi(y)=\pi_{\mathcal{P}}(y)\,(1-\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}))\leq\pi_{\mathcal{P}}(y), the sign for y∈𝒫cy\in\mathcal{P}_{c} follows. Summing gives β​π​(𝒩c)\beta\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}) over 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c} and β⁡(1−(1−π⁡(𝒩c)))=β​π​(𝒩c)\beta\big(1-(1-\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}))\big)=\beta\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c}) over 𝒫c\mathcal{P}_{c}. ∎

Implications. Proposition A.2 has three consequences, which justify the claims in Section 3.1.

  • •

    Equivalent outputs are not penalized. Only members of 𝒩c\mathcal{N}_{c}, which an oracle certifies as invalid or result-changing, are pushed down, while every positive is pushed up. An equivalent rewriting of y∗y^{*} is therefore never penalized, unlike in token-level SFT.

  • •

    Bounded, self-annealing updates. The gradient magnitude is at most β\beta and vanishes as π⁡(𝒩c)→0\pi(\mathcal{N}_{c})\to 0, so satisfied constraints stop contributing.

  • •

    Localized credit. Since rθ​(y,Mc​(y))r_{\theta}(y,M_{c}(y)) depends only on Mc​(y)M_{c}(y), other positions are supervised by ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}} alone.

Appendix B Additional Method Details

Semantic units. Figure 9 shows the semantic units of the running example. The six element types are entity (table or join path), attribute (column), value (literal and its column), aggregation (aggregate function and DISTINCT), comparison/quantifier (operator and boundary), and ordering (ORDER BY direction and LIMIT).

Dependency edges. Table 4 lists the edges of the component dependency graph GG. They are derived from SQL semantics and the key constraints of the schema.

Appendix C Implementation Details

Training. Table 5 lists the hyperparameters and Algorithm 1 (Section 3.5) summarizes the training procedure. LoRA adapters are applied to all attention and feed-forward projections.

Hyperparameter selection. We hold out 10% of the training set and grid-search λsyn,λsem,λlog∈{0.1,0.5,1.0,2.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{syn}},\lambda_{\mathrm{sem}},\lambda_{\mathrm{log}}\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0,2.0\} and β∈{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5}\beta\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5\} with the other values fixed. Figure 10 shows the sensitivity to β\beta and λlog\lambda_{\mathrm{log}} on Spider Dev.

Oracle implementation. The grammar oracle is an incremental parser for the SQLite dialect, implemented from scratch. It keeps one scope table per nested query, which records the tables, aliases, and visible columns, and covers nested queries, set operations, and CTEs. Queries outside this grammar are discarded. The execution oracle runs queries in SQLite 3.42.0 with a timeout of 5 seconds. Two queries return the same result if their outputs are equal as multisets of rows, where row order matters only when the reference contains ORDER BY, floating-point values are compared up to 2 decimal places, and NULL values are equal to each other. A query that fails or times out is treated as invalid, and its candidate is discarded. For each query pair, the counterexample generator tries up to 10 sub-databases with at most 200 mutations each. A different result on a database that satisfies the key and type constraints proves that two queries are not equivalent, so the negatives of the semantic and logical constraints are wrong by construction. Positives rest on other evidence. Semantic positives are the references, and a logical positive y′y^{\prime} must execute on all databases and pass verification.

Valid-token sets. Figure 11 shows the legal and illegal tokens that the grammar oracle derives at two decision positions.

Counterexample databases. Figure 12 shows a counterexample database for the join-path edit. The original data cannot distinguish the propagated and partially propagated queries; inserting a second, key-consistent lab section of the same course separates them.

General-purpose LLMs. All general-purpose LLMs in Section 5.3 receive the same prompt, consisting of the schema in DDL form with sample rows, the question, and an instruction to output a single SQLite query. The first SQL code block of the output is evaluated.
